content.title: How Siena basketball went from 4-28 to MAAC champion in 2 years
content.text: Siena Saints head coach Gerry McNamara: “Anyone that knows me knows why I’m here. I’m here to win." (Jim Franco/Times Union)Jim Franco/Times UnionThe Siena men’s basketball program hit rock bottom in its Division I history at 1:11 a.m. on March 13, 2024.That’s the precise time a 3-point attempt by Brendan Coyle missed at the buzzer to conclude a 67-65 loss to Niagara in the first round of the Metro Atlantic Athletic Conference Tournament at Boardwalk Hall in Atlantic City.Article continues below this adThe once-proud program finished the season at 4-28, its worst record since going Division I in 1976.One week later, Siena graduate and Clifton Park native Carmen Maciariello was relieved of his duties as head coach. Siena turned to Syracuse assistant coach Gerry McNamara, the beloved former Orange point guard, to clean up the wreckage and rebuild the Saints into a championship team.McNamara stepped up to the dais at his introductory press conference, expressing the confidence of a man who won a national championship as a Syracuse player in 2003 and went to Final Fours as an assistant in 2013 and 2016.Make the Times Union a Preferred Source on Google to see more of our journalism when you search.Add Preferred Source“Anyone that knows me knows why I’m here,” McNamara said that day in the MVP Arena atrium. “I’m here to win. Simple. That’s who I am. I am here to win. That’s all I’ve ever tried to do as a coach, a player.”Article continues below this adSiena coach Gerry McNamara, center, leads a huddle during the 2026 MAAC Tournament championship game on Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Atlantic City, N.J.Provided by Lisa SchlagerMcNamara delivered that title on Tuesday night, just three days shy of the two-year anniversary of that early morning loss to Niagara. In the same building, Boardwalk Hall, the Saints celebrated their seventh MAAC championship after a 64-54 win over Merrimack in the final.After leading the team in a worst-to-first turnaround to win the title, McNamara discussed how he was able to improve the Saints to a 14-18 win-loss record in his first season and then take another massive leap to 23-11 this season — Siena’s 50th in Division I.“I got the right kids,” McNamara said. “They’re about the right stuff … I was coming here to prove that I could win at a high level, and I got the right guys to compete at the level it takes to be competitive to try to win something.”Article continues below this adThe resurgence began with McNamara recruiting the backcourt that would eventually lead his team to a crown — Gavin Doty and Justice Shoats. Neither player was highly recruited.McNamara dipped into the NCAA transfer portal to get the 5-foot-11 Shoats, a Wilkes-Barre, Pa. native who played his first two seasons at Division II Lock Haven.McNamara landed Doty that June with the ninth and final scholarship he used for the 2024-25 team. Doty, from the Syracuse suburb of Fulton, had considered attending prep school but instead decided to play for McNamara at Siena.Siena's Justice Shoats takes a shot during the MAAC men's basketball championship game Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Atlantic City, N.J.Bill Streicher/MAACDoty’s relentless effort got Siena’s attention while he played for the Albany City Rocks in AAU tournaments.Article continues below this ad“He’s an absolute maniac, but Justice Shoats is the same way,” McNamara said. “They don’t take days off from practice. And then you factor in they’re both elite on-ball defenders.”Doty made first-team all-MAAC this season and was named tournament MVP. Shoats made second-team all-league the past two seasons.Coyle, a former walk-on who earned a scholarship, returned to play for McNamara and worked hard to develop into a more complete player than just a 3-point shooter.After the 2024-25 season ended with a last-second loss to Rider University in the first round of the MAAC Tournament, McNamara vowed to bolster a frontcourt that had been dominated inside by the Broncs. He shared that vision with Doty and Shoats right after the defeat.Article continues below this adRather than enter the transfer portal, Doty and Shoats committed to return to Siena for this season. In the era of name, image and likeness, the Saints had good money to offer both players from the athletic department’s revenue-sharing pool, which exceeds $500,000, with 85% going to men’s basketball players, according to a source. Among the contributors is former Syracuse booster Adam Weitsman, a scrap metal business mogul who’s a friend of McNamara.Siena celebrates after winning the MAAC men's basketball championship game Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Atlantic City, N.J.Bill Streicher/MAACBeyond that, Shoats said he liked the plan McNamara had to win a title.Article continues below this ad“I knew what we had coming back chemistry-wise, you know, Gav, BC and I, the big trio,” Shoats said. “And I talked to coaches over the summer and they said they were going to get a really good frontcourt, as you can see.”McNamara and his staff brought in 7-foot, 240-pound center Riley Mulvey, a graduate transfer from Rotterdam who didn’t play much in his four seasons at the University of Iowa. McNamara also brought in 6-foot-7, 245-pound Francis Folefac, a forward whose body and game don’t look like those of a freshman. The pair dominated the tournament in wins over Mount St. Mary’s, Fairfield and Merrimack. Mulvey was named to the all-tournament team.Siena also recruited freshman forward Isaiah Henderson and freshman guard Christian Jones, both of whom had their moments this season.Article continues below this adSiena had its obstacles to overcome. Starting center Tasman Goodrick, a transfer from Division II Gannon University, played only nine games because of knee injuries. Mulvey missed eight games with a concussion. Sophomore guard Reid Ducharme didn’t play because of a shoulder injury. Graduate forward Antonio Chandler started 29 games, only for Siena to discover he was NCAA-ineligible with two games left in the regular season.Regardless, the Saints are headed to their first NCAA Tournament since 2010.“It just shows our resilience, the fight, and then G-Mac taking over this job when it was a 4-28 team, to a 20-win season to champions,” Doty said. “It shows his character and how he wants to win.”Article continues below this adMarch 14, 2026Mark Singelais covers Siena basketball, UAlbany lacrosse, horse racing and other sports.
